question: Given the concerns about the environmental consequences of concrete, the world’s third largest source of carbon dioxide pollution, the industrial practices that contribute to this problem need to be examined. One of the uses of concrete that merits particular attention is wind turbines, which are presented as a source of green energy.

Wind turbines sit on a concrete base made of hundreds of tonnes of concrete, so they contribute to demand for this polluting material. In addition, the short lifespan of the blades (20 years) and the fact that they cannot be recycled raise concerns about long-term waste management. In France, wind energy is interesting first and foremost for developers, who receive EUR 4 billion annually from the government.

And because of its intermittent nature, it is often linked to coal-fired power plants, which are necessarily polluting. In this context, it essential that we question the environmental sustainability of wind turbines and consider possible alternatives to reduce the influence of concrete in the European energy transition.

In view of these concerns about the environmental consequences of concrete and its use in the construction of wind turbines, what measures does the Commission intend to take to promote genuinely sustainable and ecological energy solutions in the EU?
answer: Renewable energy sources such as wind power are central in the energy transition of the EU. They play a key role in the achievement of the EU greenhouse gas emissions target for 2030 and the objective of climate-neutrality by 2050. Their deployment brings multiple environmental, economic and social benefits and is promoted at EU level mainly through Directive (EU) 2018/2001 (1).

Whilst concrete is used in almost all forms of energy production, wind energy is among the electricity generation sources with the lowest carbon intensity (2). The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has found that average lifecycle emissions from wind are 1% those of coal or 2% of gas power production (3).

The European Strategy for Energy System Integration (4) describes how the variable production of certain technologies can be absorbed in a more integrated energy system through the coordinated planning and operation of the energy system as a whole, while remaining resource-efficient and avoiding pollution and biodiversity loss.

The EU environmental legislation fully applies to wind turbines, including Article 4 of the Waste Framework Directive (5) that sets out the mandatory Waste Hierarchy. Accordingly, waste prevention (e.g. re-use) has to be prioritised, followed by preparing for re-use and recycling. Incineration, including with energy recovery, and landfilling are at the bottom of the Waste Hierarchy.

The experience with end-of-life treatment is very limited to date because only few of the first installed wind turbines have reached their end-of-life stage. Nevertheless, currently about 85-90% of the total mass of a wind turbine (i.e. the foundation, tower and components in the nacelle) can be and is recycled (6).
